blocks.etymology: Ellipsis of speak of the devil and he shall appear, which can be traced back to “talk of the Devil, and he’s presently at your elbow”, attested in 1666. The idea behind this (namely, that mentioning a dangerous creature may cause it to appear) is found in many cultures around the world; see taboo avoidance.

examples: A: You know who would appreciate this? Tom. B: Speak of the devil! Look who just walked in!
wiktionary.gloss: An expression sometimes used when a person mentioned in the current conversation happens to arrive on the scene.

blocks.etymology: First attested as a filled pause in the early 18th century, as a euphemism in the mid-19th century.

wiktionary.gloss: Expression signifying a pause or hesitation.

examples:
A: I can’t go to the party because... you know...
B: Your mom is still mad at you, huh?
A: Yeah...
wiktionary.gloss: Expression used to imply meaning, rather than say it, such as when a person is embarrassed.

examples: But I guess that's life, you know?
I just wasn't into it, you know?
wiktionary.gloss: Used as a rhetorical question to confirm agreement, knowing or understanding at the end of a statement.

examples: You know, he's actually pretty nice.
wiktionary.gloss: Used to introduce information.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see you, know.
